# TO21733133

#TO #footankle #gaitcycle
Chapter: Regional Orthopedics MCQs — Clinical Examination And Gait

## Question

False option regarding gait

## Options

1. During stance phase maximum force for further movement is generated by heel
2. When runner is slow, the heel strikes first but when running fast, the forefoot strikes first
3. Tibio talar joint pronation is there when foot is on ground
4. Anterior pelvic tilt upto 100 is acceptable during stance phase

## Correct option

**1. During stance phase maximum force for further movement is generated by heel**

## Answer explanation

Ans: A

EXPLANATION: -
This question on biomechanics of gait cycle needs discussion of each option in a sequential manner.
CHOICE A: During loading (heel strike to foot flat) – The foot supinates, the rearfoot (heel) contacts the ground in slight inversion (00-50). At heel strike, the pelvis is level, in slight anterior tilt (10°), and internally rotated; the hip is externally rotated (5-10°) and flexed (20-30°); and the knee is flexed (10°). Due to the laterally directed line of the GRF produced by heel strike, a cascade of events occurs to assist shock absorption. First, the rearfoot begins to evert, accompanied by tibia and femoral (hip) internal rotation, and hip adduction. This is combined with knee flexion, which peaks at around 45° as a result of the GRF line passing posterior to the knee joint. Each of these motions is controlled by eccentric muscle activity which helps to dissipate the GRF. In addition, there may be contralateral pelvic drop, although this should be minimal (approximately 5°). The gluteal musculature should actively control this motion and further dissipate the GRF. Therefore, the heel is responsible for force acceptance and shock absorption and not force generation. So, choice A is false.

CHOICE B: Changing from a heel strike to a forefoot strike pattern: This is the adaptation to fast speed running. This means that the ankle joint is more compliant and able to absorb GRF in the sagittal plane, and can lead to a reduction in vertical GRF following foot strike (see image below). Additionally, forefoot striking has also been reported to reduce knee and hip joint loads. However, at the ankle-foot this could indicate potential detrimental increases to tissue stresses, which fits with many anecdotal reports of Achilles tendinopathy, plantar fasciopathy and metatarsal stress fractures as a result of transitioning from heel to forefoot strike.

![[TO21733133-1.png]]

CHOICE C: Tibiotalar pronation is a 3-dimensional motion of the ankle joint that involves the positioning of the foot in stance phase. Pronation of the foot involves dorsiflexion, eversion and abduction. It’s a combination of these movements that positions the sole of the foot to face laterally. Now imagine the midstance (foot flat to heel off) phase of gait cycle. The beginning is indicated by the “forefoot” making contact with the ground, normally in a neutral transverse plane position (i.e. not abducted or adducted). Lower limb biomechanical function during midstance involves a transition from biomechanics required for shock absorption following loading, to biomechanics required for propulsion. During this time, the ankle moves towards maximal dorsiflexion (approximately 20°) to allow forward motion of the tibia and the centre of mass (COM) to pass over the stance leg. At the same time, the hip and knee are moving from flexion towards extended positions, assisting forward motion of the body's COM. Foot reaches maximum pronation after maximal ankle dorsiflexion has been reached as the body’s COM has passes anterior to the stance limb. Peak rearfoot eversion reaches approximately 10° and peak forefoot abduction approximately 5° in stance phase.

CHOICE D: During the early stance phase of loading, from heel strike to foot flat, anterior pelvic tilt of 100 is acceptable. Excessive anterior pelvic tilting can place excessive strain on the lumbar spine and/or the hamstring musculature, and may impair gluteal function.
